seoDescription: 2,784 SaaS M&A deals in twelve months, 54 percent vertical software, and the median PE firm saw 18.4 percent of its own market. What coverage costs.

sections.name: The market is busy. Most of it goes unseen.

items.text: The market is busy. Most of it goes unseen.

Twelve months of SaaS transactions, more than half of them vertical software, and a benchmark that measures how much of its own market a buyer actually sees. The answer for the median private equity firm is fewer than one deal in five.

The median private equity firm sees fewer than one deal in five of the ones available inside its own stated market.

How this was measured: the study took 177 private equity firms. For each one, it listed the deals completed in the industries and sizes that firm says it targets, each with a private equity buyer and a sell-side advisor, and counted how many of those the firm saw. sections.name: No buyer sees most of its market. The question is who decides which...

items.text: No buyer sees most of its market. The question is who decides which part you see.

The benchmark takes a private equity firm’s own stated criteria, lists every closed transaction in those industries and sizes that had a private equity buyer and a sell-side advisor, and counts how many of them the firm saw. It is a measure of the market the firm says it wants, not of the whole market. A firm that saw 18.4 percent of its own stated market did not see the other 81.6 percent, and the sell-side advisors who ran those processes decided who did.

The figure falls as deals get smaller. Firms buying at $10 million to $49 million of enterprise value saw a median of 9.0 percent. In the lower middle market the sell side is more fragmented, the processes are narrower, and a buyer’s coverage depends on relationships with a longer list of smaller advisors. The median firm counted 199 of them as sources.
Why vertical software is harder to cover

Vertical software is sold by sector. The buyer of a dental practice management company is rarely the buyer of a freight audit platform, and the advisor who knows one sector rarely knows the other. A buyer with criteria across ten industries is trying to be known in ten separate markets at once, each with its own owners, its own acquirers and its own reasons a deal breaks. The share of SaaS transactions that are vertical software passed half in 2026, so the harder half of the market is now the larger half.
No buyer sees most of its own market. The question is who decides which part of it you see.

Three things, in order. Criteria on file with the people who map a sector before anyone goes to market, so that a fit is recognized when it appears. Owner relationships built ahead of a process, so that a buyer is already known when the owner decides. And the evidence on a company assembled before a letter of intent, so that the time a buyer spends under exclusivity is spent on a deal that can close. Capital Row keeps a buyer’s criteria on file and confirms them each quarter. A dedicated search in one sector is by exception.
